name: Toda
script: Unwritten (Tamil and IPA used in transcription)
lead: Toda (endonym: Oḷy Mōt) is a language spoken by the pastoral Toda community in the Nilgiri Hills of Tamil Nadu, India.[1] First documented systematically by M. B. Emeneau between 1935 and 1938, Toda is noted in comparative linguistics for its phonological divergence from neighboring languages, preserving a 16-vowel system and multiple apical, laminal, and retroflex sibilants and trills.[1][2]
history:
The Toda people inhabit small hamlets known as mod (munds) situated at elevations above 2,000 meters on the Nilgiri plateau.[1] Comparative reconstruction by Bhadriraju Krishnamurti places the split of Proto-Toda-Kota from pre-Tamil during the early first millennium BCE, followed by geographical isolation in the upper Nilgiris.[2]

Traditional Toda society organized its economy around the sacred water buffalo (īr) and ritual dairies.[1] The 2001 Census of India recorded 1,560 speakers; UNESCO and the Government of India classify the language as Critically Endangered due to educational shift toward Tamil and English.[3][4]
phonology: Toda has 35+ consonant phonemes, caused historically by the syncope of non-initial short vowels.[1][2] It distinguishes three voiceless/voiced sibilant-affricate series, voiceless laterals (/ɬ/, /ɭ̊/), and three distinct rhotics: alveolar trill /r/, alveolar tap/trill /r̪/, and retroflex trill /ɽr/.[1] The vowel inventory comprises 16 phonemes (8 qualities × short/long), including front rounded vowels /y, yː/ (written ü, ǖ in Emeneau's notation) and central unrounded /ɨ, ɨː/ (written ï, ï̄).[1]
syntax: Toda is a head-final, Subject–Object–Verb (SOV) agglutinative language.[1] Nominal stems inflect for case via suffixes attached to an oblique stem (e.g., accusative -n, dative -k, ablative -sn).[1] Finite verbs carry tense-aspect-mood suffixes followed by pronominal person-number-gender markers.[1][2]

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Personal Pronouns & Numerals
lessons.intro: Toda retains the inclusive/exclusive distinction in first-person plural pronouns (Emeneau 1984: 72–76, 98).<sup>[1]</sup>

quiz.q: Which Toda pronoun denotes first-person plural inclusive ('we, including the addressee')?
quiz.a: om (/om/) — distinct from em (/em/, 'we excluding the addressee').

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Swadesh Nouns & Nilgiri Ecology
lessons.intro: Core lexical items from Emeneau (1984) and the Dravidian Etymological Dictionary (Burrow & Emeneau 1984).<sup>[1][5]</sup>

quiz.q: What are the Toda terms for 'water' and 'milk'?

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Verbal Roots & Case Suffixes
lessons.intro: Toda verbs distinguish Root 1 (uninflected base) and Root 2 (past/participial stem formed via alveolar/dental suffixation).<sup>[1]</sup>

quiz.q: How is the dative form of mod ('village/mund') constructed?
quiz.a: By attaching the dative suffix -k: mod-k ('to the hamlet').

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Interlinear Glossed Sentences
lessons.intro: Morphological analysis using standard Leipzig Glossing Rules (Emeneau 1984).<sup>[1]</sup>
